hook.text: An average is meant to tell you the typical value. So take ten salaries at a small company, from forty-two to sixty-five thousand.

centers.text: Their mean is fifty-three point seven thousand. Their median, the middle value, is fifty-three and a half. Almost the same.

ceo.text: Now the CEO walks in, earning a million.

jump.text: The mean leaps to a hundred and thirty-nine point seven thousand. The median just moves to fifty-five.

nobody.text: Ten of the eleven people earn less than the mean. It describes almost nobody in the room.

balance.text: That's because the mean is a balance point. Put one heavy value far out, and the balance point slides toward it.

middle.text: The median only asks who's in the middle. It doesn't care how far out the CEO sits.

tail-in.text: And money nearly always has a tail like that.

orders.text: Here are five hundred customer orders. Most are modest, with a long tail stretching off to the right.

median.text: The median order is about twenty-three dollars.

mean.text: The mean is twenty-six fifty-eight. The tail drags it up.

alarm.text: So a mean above the median is a free alarm for skew. The wider the gap, the more you should lead with the median.

right.text: Which center is right? That depends on the data.

symmetric.text: Symmetric, with no wild values? The mean uses everything, and works well.

skewed.text: Skewed, like incomes, prices and wait times? The median is the honest typical value.

categories.text: Categories? Only the most common one, the mode, makes sense.

peaks.text: And two peaks? Then no single center will do.

spread-in.text: But even the right center hides how much the values move.

delivery.text: Two delivery services both average thirty minutes.

swing.text: One always arrives between twenty-eight and thirty-two. The other swings from five minutes to fifty-five.

same.text: Same center, completely different experience. What differs is the spread.

deviations.text: To measure it, take each delivery's distance from the mean. For the steady service, they run from minus two to plus two, and they cancel out to zero.

square.text: So square them first. Now they add up to twelve.

variance.text: Divide by nine, one less than the count, and that's the variance.

erratic.text: For the erratic service, it's almost eighteen.

divisor.text: So why nine, and not ten? Because the distances are measured from the sample's own mean.

closest.text: And that mean sits closer to its own points than any other number does.

truth.text: These five values come from a population whose true mean is zero. Measure from the truth instead, and the squares grow.

small.text: So around the sample's mean, the squares run small. Divide by n, the number of values, and you'd underestimate the spread.

measured.text: Over four thousand samples of five, dividing by n comes out about twenty percent low. Dividing by n minus one lands on the truth.

libs.text: That's why numpy and pandas disagree. numpy divides by n unless you ask, and pandas by n minus one.

robust-in.text: Squares have one more weakness. A single wild value can swamp them.

incomes.text: Take ten incomes. Nine fall between thirty-eight and a hundred and twenty. The tenth is nine thousand.

sd.text: The standard deviation leaps to over two thousand eight hundred.

iqr.text: The interquartile range only measures the middle half, from the first quartile to the third, a quarter and three quarters of the way up. It's fourteen, whatever the top earner makes.

mad.text: Its cousin, the median absolute deviation, takes the typical distance from the median. Here, eight.

pair.text: So pair them. A mean goes with a standard deviation, and a median goes with the IQR.

shape-in.text: Still, a center and a spread can't tell you what the data looks like.

shape.text: For that, you need its shape. And skew is named for the long tail, not for the peak.

right-tail.text: A tail to the right drags the mean above the median.

left-tail.text: A tail to the left drags it below. Symmetric data keeps the two together.

two-peaks.text: Two peaks usually mean two groups in one column. Mix the heights of two groups, and the mean lands in the valley between them.

tails-in.text: And the tails matter as much as the middle.

tails.text: Draw twenty thousand values from a normal distribution, and just one lands beyond four standard deviations.

heavy.text: From a heavy-tailed one, a hundred and twenty-seven do.

routine.text: Heavy tails make rare events routine. Financial returns, insurance losses and network delays all live out there.

outlier-in.text: So a value far out isn't automatically a mistake.

outlier.text: An outlier is a value far from the rest. That's all the word means.

kinds.text: It might be an error, like a typo. It might be a placeholder, like minus nine ninety-nine for missing. Or it might be real... your biggest customer, or a fraud.

flag.text: Now take two hundred skewed incomes, plus two genuine high earners. The box-plot fences flag six points. The z-score rule flags just two.

ordinary.text: Four of those six are simply the long tail of ordinary incomes.

verdict.text: So a flag is a question, not a verdict. Find out why a point is out there, and then decide: fix an error, treat a placeholder as missing, keep what's real.

plot-in.text: And the surest way to find out is to look.

dino.text: Here are thirteen datasets. They share their means, their standard deviations and their correlation, to within a hundredth.

plot.text: Now plot them. One is a dinosaur. Others are a star, a circle, and a set of lines.

credit.text: Alberto Cairo drew the dinosaur. In twenty seventeen, Justin Matejka and George Fitzmaurice built the other twelve to match its numbers.

lossy.text: A summary is a lossy copy. The plot keeps what it threw away.

bins-in.text: But a plot makes choices too.

bins.text: A histogram's bin width is a knob. These are the SAME thousand values, in five bins, then twenty, then eighty.

wide.text: Wide bins blur the shape into a few blocks. Narrow ones turn every wobble into a peak.

believe.text: Nothing in the data says which to believe. So look at more than one.

plots.text: Which plot, when? For the shape of one variable, a histogram, at a few bin widths.

ecdf.text: To read off percentiles with nothing to tune, an ECDF: the share of values at or below each point.

box.text: To compare groups, box plots. But a box only knows its quartiles, so it can't show a second peak.

violin.text: A violin can. It draws the shape the box leaves out.

habit.text: Whatever you pick, plot FIRST, and summarize second.

next.text: A summary and a plot describe the data you have. To reason about data you haven't seen, you need probability... starting with what a probability even means.

root.text: Its square root, back in minutes, is the standard deviation... about one point two.

rules.text: The fences sit one and a half times the IQR past the quartiles. The z-score rule flags anything three standard deviations from the mean.
